I knew a fair offer would not have a huge bonus for me, but I was willing to try for a second offer after my first counteroffer was accepted. In order to increase my bonus, I adjusted the start date and increased the amount of days of remote work. I did not expect these changes to be opposed, and I was correct when my partner accepted my second counteroffer.
responses.q32: I did not feel stuck with the negotiations because I saw my partner improve her offer the second time.
responses.q33: I would have tried for a third offer if my partner had been more talkative, but I felt her English skills were more limited than mine. She is from a different cultural background than me, and I thought she might have English as her second language. Her first offer only had three conditions listed, which made me think it would be hard to negotiate for a significantly better offer since I had fewer additional conditions to negotiate with in terms of intangibles. I would have to come up with other ideas besides mentoring and offering to help with the company recruiting fair, and I was not sure if it would be worth the extra time and effort to do so. I am usually more talkative in real life when it comes to negotiating, and part of it is because unlike a simulation, I have actual goals I want to accomplish where I am more willing to spend more time to achieve them. These goals have often involved customer service or helping a friend out by booking or cancelling medical appointments. It is not a criticism of this type of study since it is an acknowledgement of the limitations of negotiation simulations. A negotation based on a job offer is ideal since it provides a mix of qualitative and quantitative data and requests to take into consideration. Negotiations based solely on qualitative or quantitative requests provide less robust research data in simulation studies, although such negotations exist in real life.
